subject: modelfit worse through contraining intercepts z-standardized variables

messages.author: aeba240e2095f06a
messages.subject: modelfit worse through contraining intercepts z-standardized variables
parts:
Hello everyone,
I am fitting a model with several z-standardized variables. I thought that constraining their intercepts to zero would necessarily improve my model fit. This is not the case and I was wondering if anyone knows why.
The RMSEA was quite good .05 [.04 .05], same for the SRMR .04. CFI wasn't exactly good (.78) but the RMSEA of the null model is smaller than .158.
If I don't specify the intercepts to be zero, the estimates are all near zero, as they should be.
Thanks for any advice.

Best,

Kathrin

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: modelfit worse through contraining intercepts z-standardized variables
parts: I am fitting a model with several z-standardized variables.

Don't do that, unless you understand how to constrain residual variances such that the model-implied total variances == 1 (which is fixed for correlations).  Otherwise, you will have inflated Type I error rates.

https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0033-2909.105.2.317
I thought that constraining their intercepts to zero would necessarily improve my model fit. This is not the case and I was wondering if anyone knows why.

The sample means of z-scores calculated using sample M & SD are 0 by definition.  But means are not model parameters.  Intercepts are expected values (means) of the outcome when its predictor(s) equal(s) zero.  Not sure what your model looks like, but if it is just a CFA with latent mean(s) fixed to zero, then it would make sense for indicator intercepts to also be zero (within the bounds of machine precision, so zero to 15 digits or so) because the expected value of an outcome is its grand mean when holding all predictors at their grand means.  But with more complicated models, that would not necessarily be the case.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
